text.title: Unattended Automation Failure Modes
text.summary: Six ways an automation layer becomes the problem it was bought to solve, each with the observable symptom and the rule that prevents it.

failure.symptom: A workflow runtime has been running for months. It holds two workflows, one of which is the tutorial. Its updates are the only maintenance it generates.
failure.cause: It was installed against imagined workflows rather than an observed failure, and the imagined ones were never built.
failure.prevention: Name one dated trigger the current arrangement failed to serve. No dated failure means `chosen_surface: none` until one occurs.

failure.symptom: The workflow is triggered by the operator clicking Run. The tool has replaced a command with a browser tab.
failure.cause: The gate was never applied: every trigger had a human present, so the agent session already covered the whole surface.
failure.prevention: Enumerate triggers with `human_present`. If none is false, install nothing — that is the analysis succeeding.

failure.symptom: Half a workflow is built before anyone discovers the tool cannot run the binary the whole thing was for, and the remaining path is an enterprise plan or an HTTP service you now have to run yourself.
failure.cause: The exec requirement was assumed rather than verified, and it is architectural: a sandbox that blocks exec is the product's security model, not a setting.
failure.prevention: Set `needs_local_exec` before choosing. As of 2026-08-04 that requirement alone eliminates Make, Dify and Flowise, and restricts n8n to self-hosted with the node re-enabled.

failure.symptom: Something ran twice last Tuesday. Something else has not run since April and nobody noticed, because each surface's owner assumed the other had it.
failure.cause: A workflow runtime was added beside an existing scheduler instead of replacing it, so there is no single readable inventory of what fires unattended.
failure.prevention: Exactly one surface, named. A second one goes in `rejected_surfaces`, never alongside.

failure.symptom: A nightly job that has produced no output and no error for three weeks. Nothing alerted, because nothing failed.
failure.cause: The host sleeps. An absent run raises no error, so the failure mode is silence and silence is not monitored by default.
failure.prevention: Declare the host and require `always-on`. If none exists, provision one and state its monthly cost in currency, or fall back to `none`.

failure.symptom: An automated run published sixty times overnight, or spent against an API key until the quota ended it. Somebody had to find the workflow before they could stop it.
failure.cause: No declared blast radius and no stop switch operable without reading the workflow — the first failures of unattended work happen with nobody watching.
failure.prevention: Declare what a run may write, publish and spend, and name a halt a human can operate cold.
